title: ROWS vs RANGE Window Frames
description: Explain why two running-total queries return different numbers and which frame to use for ties.

data.text: Two developers wrote a running-total query over the same `Sales` table and got different answers on days where more than one sale has the same date. One used `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, the other wrote no frame clause at all. Explain the difference and show which to use.

data.title: SQL Solution
data.code:
-- RANGE (also the implicit default when you specify ORDER BY and no frame):
-- all rows with the SAME value of the ORDER BY key are peers, so they share a total.
SELECT
    SaleDate,
    Amount,
    SUM(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY SaleDate) AS RangeRunningTotal
FROM Sales;

-- ROWS: strictly physical row-by-row accumulation, no peer grouping.
SELECT
    SaleDate,
    Amount,
    SUM(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY SaleDate ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
        AS RowsRunningTotal
FROM Sales;

-- Deterministic answer: break ties with a unique column and use ROWS.
SELECT
    SaleId,
    SaleDate,
    Amount,
    SUM(Amount) OVER (
        ORDER BY SaleDate, SaleId
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS RunningTotal
FROM Sales;

data.title: Explanation
data.text: With `RANGE`, all rows that are **peers** on the `ORDER BY` key get the same aggregated value — so three sales on 2024-03-01 all show the total through the end of that day. With `ROWS`, the total advances one physical row at a time. The default frame when you write `ORDER BY` without a frame is `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, which is why the frameless query behaved like the `RANGE` version. **Use `ROWS` and add a unique tiebreaker** whenever you want a running total: `ROWS` is cheaper (no peer detection) and, with a unique sort key, deterministic and repeatable.
